findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

findings.description: calcified focus consistent with an old, benign granuloma

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. Small calcified granuloma in the right frontal lobe without mass effect or surrounding edema.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.
Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

citations: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190
action_criteria.expected_evidence: Hoover sign and dragging gait in the right leg; spasticity, reflexes and ataxia unchanged from her MS baseline
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: The examination makes the diagnosis and frames the imaging question: new pyramidal or cerebellar signs would point to a relapse or PML, while positive functional signs with an unchanged baseline point to functional weakness.

citations: McGuigan C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2016;87:117-125
action_criteria.expected_evidence: Lesion load unchanged from 6 months earlier, nothing enhancing, no PML pattern on FLAIR or diffusion
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI with gadolinium for relapse and PML
action_criteria.rationale: A new deficit on natalizumab with a JC virus index of 2.8 after 4 years needs MRI with FLAIR, DWI and gadolinium to answer two questions the examination cannot: a new or enhancing MS lesion and PML. Expert consensus places her in the high-risk stratum, in which any new symptom is imaged.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count and chemistry, which neither support nor refute the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Blood count and metabolic panel
action_criteria.rationale: Defensible as routine monitoring on natalizumab; no blood test bears on the cause of the new weakness.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No new cord lesion; it does not change the diagnosis made on examination
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI
action_criteria.rationale: A cord relapse would not show on the brain MRI; unchanged reflexes and tone, positive functional signs and normal walking when unobserved argue against one, so a spine MRI is defensible but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction that alters management; sedation from lorazepam noted
action_criteria.label: Medication review
action_criteria.rationale: Natalizumab and as-needed lorazepam do not interact; lorazepam can worsen balance, but nothing in the list changes the diagnosis or plan.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Profile of comorbid mood, anxiety and somatic symptom burden to guide therapy; no bearing on the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of mood, anxiety and dissociation
action_criteria.rationale: A battery with performance-validity measures can characterise the comorbidity that treatment will target; it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only; the diagnosis and plan for this patient do not depend on a literature result
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on functional neurological disorder
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on positive diagnosis and treatment can inform the explanation and the referral; no step of the diagnostic work-up depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Treat the episode as an MS relapse with high-dose corticosteroids.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional right leg weakness coexisting with stable relapsing-remitting MS) based on the right Hoover sign and dragging monoplegic gait with an unchanged MS baseline and a stable gadolinium MRI, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).

Do not change her disease-modifying therapy for the functional weakness; refer the PML risk back to her MS team, since a JC virus index of 2.8 after 4 years of natalizumab calls for a risk-benefit review (extended-interval dosing or a switch) and 3- to 4-monthly MRI surveillance while she remains on it.

avoided_actions.rationale: No syncope, palpitations or abnormal vital signs; an ECG answers no question raised by a leg weakness with positive functional signs.
No embolic or structural cardiac question: the deficit has positive functional signs and the MRI shows no new lesion.
There are no events of altered awareness or syncope to correlate with a rhythm.
The questions on natalizumab (relapse, PML) need MRI with gadolinium; a CT answers neither and adds radiation.
FDG-PET has no role in a functional deficit or in the relapse and PML questions, which the MRI answers.
Her weakness is central with positive functional signs; EMG and nerve conduction studies answer no question and a normal result reinforces the search for an organic cause.
Evoked potentials add nothing to a known MS diagnosis and cannot explain non-dermatomal sensory loss.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder with functional right leg weakness, coexisting with stable relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis

differential.key_features: Stable for 4 years on natalizumab; the new weakness shows the Hoover sign and a dragging gait, with no new pyramidal sign or reflex change, and the gadolinium MRI shows no new or enhancing lesion. A cord relapse is not imaged but is argued against by unchanged tone and reflexes and normal walking when unobserved.
A JC virus index of 2.8 after 4 years of natalizumab is a high-risk stratum, but the MRI shows no new FLAIR or diffusion lesion and the deficit has positive functional signs.

Feigning is conscious and cannot be separated from FND by examination signs; her ongoing medical leave is noted, but she herself says the episode is unlike her relapses and is distressed by it, which argues against it.

key_clinical_evidence: Positive signs of functional right leg weakness: Hoover sign (hip extension 2/5 directly, 4/5 with contralateral hip flexion) and a dragging monoplegic gait.
Her MS baseline (right leg spasticity, hyperreflexia, heel-shin ataxia) is unchanged and no new pathological reflex is present.
The gadolinium MRI shows a stable lesion load, no enhancing lesion and no features of PML, the two questions natalizumab raises.
A JC virus index of 2.8 after 4 years on natalizumab is why imaging is indicated here and is a matter for her MS team; it does not make the weakness organic.
She says the episode is unlike her relapses; onset after a night of caregiving is context, neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: FND commonly coexists with MS; the new weakness has positive functional signs, the baseline signs are unchanged and the MRI shows no new or enhancing lesion.
red_herrings.data_point: Established relapsing-remitting MS with right leg signs from prior lesions
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attributing any new deficit to an MS relapse and treating it with steroids
red_herrings.location: Past medical history and neurological examination

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The index sets PML risk; it is not evidence that the current symptom is PML. The MRI with FLAIR, DWI and gadolinium answers the question.
red_herrings.data_point: JC virus antibody index 2.8 on natalizumab
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchoring on PML and pursuing a lumbar puncture for JC virus PCR despite a stable MRI

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND; the diagnosis rests on the positive signs.
red_herrings.data_point: Anxiety disorder treated with as-needed lorazepam
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a psychological label without positive signs, or dismissing the weakness because she is anxious

sequence_constraints.reason: The examination comes first and frames what the MRI must answer: relapse or PML if new signs are found, a functional deficit if positive functional signs are found (Espay 2018).

findings.result: Right hip extension 2/5 on direct testing, returning to 4/5 during contralateral hip flexion against resistance.
The right leg is dragged behind with the foot kept on the floor, worse than her baseline spastic gait.
Mild right leg spasticity, right leg hyperreflexia and right heel-shin ataxia unchanged from her documented baseline; no new pathological reflexes.
Non-dermatomal right leg sensory loss unlike her prior MS sensory pattern, and walking at her usual pace in the corridor when unaware of being observed; not counted as rule-in signs.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: Hoover sign and dragging monoplegic gait on the right. The new weakness is inconsistent with a structural lesion; her baseline MS signs are unchanged.

general.proposed: Natalizumab 300 mg IV every 4 weeks; Lorazepam 0.5 mg as needed for acute anxiety
general.summary: No clinically significant interaction between natalizumab and lorazepam. Natalizumab carries a PML boxed warning; lorazepam sedates and impairs balance.
warnings: Natalizumab: boxed warning for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy; risk rises with treatment beyond 2 years, prior immunosuppressant use and a higher anti-JC virus antibody index. Concomitant immunosuppressants add to the risk; none is listed.
Lorazepam: sedation, impaired balance and falls; dependence with regular use.

labs.interpretation: All results are within reference ranges.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Review and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder from motor signs of high specificity, and physiotherapy whose effect on the trial's primary outcome was modest; a later revision of the diagnosis is uncommon.

additional_observations: Technique: T1, T2, FLAIR, DWI/ADC and SWI, with T1 after intravenous gadolinium. Comparison: brain MRI 6 months ago.
No new or enlarging T2/FLAIR lesion.
No new subcortical or juxtacortical FLAIR lesion, no new diffusion abnormality and no punctate T2 lesions.

findings.location: Periventricular and juxtacortical white matter, left corona radiata along the corticospinal tract, right middle cerebellar peduncle (known MS lesions)

signal_characteristics.T2_FLAIR: Hyperintense; number and size unchanged from the MRI 6 months ago

mri.impression: 1. Stable demyelinating lesion burden compared with the MRI 6 months ago: no new or enlarging T2/FLAIR lesion and no gadolinium-enhancing lesion. 2. No imaging features of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. 3. No acute intracranial abnormality.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Functional weakness in a patient with established MS on natalizumab and a high JC virus index: the agent must make the positive diagnosis from the signs and still answer the relapse and PML questions with one gadolinium MRI, without further testing.
metadata.notes: Functional right leg weakness superimposed on stable RRMS on natalizumab; gadolinium MRI excludes a new or enhancing lesion and PML.

patient.chief_complaint: Worsening right leg weakness — worse than baseline MS

medications.indication: Relapsing-remitting MS — last infusion 3 weeks ago

past_medical_history: Multiple sclerosis (RRMS), diagnosed 8 years ago, on natalizumab — stable for 4 years (EDSS 2.0)

social_history.occupation: Middle school teacher, currently on medical leave
social_history.recent_stressor: Mother diagnosed with early dementia 2 months ago; caregiving burden; loss of routine following medical leave for MS monitoring

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. N is a 47-year-old middle school teacher with relapsing-remitting MS diagnosed 8 years ago, stable on natalizumab for 4 years (EDSS 2.0), who presents with a 10-day history of right leg weakness beyond her established baseline. She reports that this episode feels different from her prior MS relapses, which typically involved sensory symptoms or brief worsening of balance. The weakness started abruptly one morning after a particularly difficult night caring for her mother, who has early dementia. She is on medical leave from her teaching position for MS monitoring appointments. Her last natalizumab infusion was 3 weeks ago. Her last brain MRI, 6 months ago, was stable. Her JC virus antibody index at her routine check 3 months ago was 2.8.

neurological_exam.additional: Right leg weakness worse than her documented MS baseline, variable with distraction; baseline right leg spasticity, hyperreflexia, and mild heel-shin ataxia from prior MS are unchanged. No new pathological reflexes.
neurological_exam.coordination: Baseline mild right heel-shin ataxia (from prior MS lesion) — no change.
neurological_exam.gait: Dragging right leg worse than baseline. Observed to walk at baseline MS pace in corridor when unaware of observation.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Tearful. 'I know what an MS relapse feels like and this is not it.'
neurological_exam.motor: Right leg apparent weakness 2/5. POSITIVE Hoover sign right leg. Right leg strength 4/5 on distracted examination. Left leg normal. No new spasticity or hyperreflexia compared to prior (baseline EDSS 2.0 with mild right leg spasticity from prior MS lesion).
neurological_exam.reflexes: Baseline right leg hyperreflexia (from prior MS) — no change from documented baseline. No new pathological reflexes.
neurological_exam.sensory: Right leg sensory loss — non-anatomical, inconsistent with prior MS distribution.
